title: Advanced JSON Processing
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Advanced JSON Processing.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to json path expressions.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Advanced JSON Processing. Its primary job is to help you query document-shaped JSON and searchable text while choosing when relational columns or extensions are better. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing advanced json processing teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: query document-shaped JSON and searchable text while choosing when relational columns or extensions are better. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Advanced JSON Processing
content_blocks.safety_note: Use JSONB for documented document semantics, not as an excuse to omit relational constraints.

content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Advanced JSON Processing”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “JSON path expressions”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “JSON path expressions”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Advanced JSON Processing, with an explanation of “JSON path expressions”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Advanced JSON Processing fits into the broader goal to query document-shaped JSON and searchable text while choosing when relational columns or extensions are better.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: JSON path expressions, SQL/JSON functionality, Processing JSON query results.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
